title: Salerno
topic: The imperative: giving orders and directions

{"lessons": ["

Forming the imperative

You'll need it to ask for directions, and above all to understand the answer. English has a single form (“Turn left!”), but Italian has one for a friend (tu), one for formal address (Lei), and one for a group (voi).

parlareprenderedormirefinire
tuparlaprendidormifinisci
Leiparliprendadormafinisca
noiparliamoprendiamodormiamofiniamo
voiparlateprendetedormitefinite

The trap: the vowels swap. For -are verbs, tu = -a and Lei = -i. For the others, it's the reverse: tu = -i, Lei = -a.

Common irregulars

tuLei
andareva' (vai)vada
farefa' (fai)faccia
dareda' (dai)dia
diredi'dica
staresta' (stai)stia
venirevienivenga
esseresiisia
avereabbiabbia
", "

Negation and pronouns

In the negative, the tu form uses the infinitive. The other persons don't change.

Non parlare! Non parlate! Non parli!Don't talk! (to a friend, to a group, then formal)

Where does the pronoun go?

With tu, noi and voi, it attaches to the end of the verb. With Lei, it stays in front.

Prendilo! Scrivetemi! Andiamoci!Take it! Write to me! Let's go (there)!
Lo prenda! Mi dica!Take it! Tell me! (Lei)

With the short forms (va', fa', da', di', sta'), the pronoun's consonant doubles: dimmi (tell me), fallo (do it), dammi (give me), vacci (go there).

Reflexive verbs follow the same rule: siediti (sit down, to a friend), sedetevi (sit down, to a group), si sieda (Lei).
